📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most prominent figures of the so-called Bluenami was not a candidate on the ballot, but rather a Twitch streamer and political commentator: Hasan Piker.

Recent findings suggest that this year Hasan was involved in dozens of races across the country, campaigning for progressive candidates like Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed. But you’re probably more likely to associate Hasan’s name with what other people have had to say about him—from Fox News commentators to more established members of the Democratic Party.

Hasan regularly courts controversy on both his hours-long Twitch streams, where he’s said things like “America deserved 9/11,” and social media, where he’s written that Hamas “is a thousand times better than” Israel. He claims he’s often taken out of context, and that his audience knows what he really means—and where he stands. In his mind, he’s a leftist provocateur, maybe, but one who understands the importance of working-class values and electoral strategy.

According to recent reports, while Hasan has walked back some of his more inflammatory language, his rhetoric raises the question: Is he a liability to the cause he champions? Or is he successfully reaching the critical audience—namely, young men—that helped elect the wave of progressives poised to take office in January?

It has been revealed that with 2028 on the horizon, I wanted to know how Hasan thinks about his growing platform, and if he sees his role shifting in the media landscape. What responsibility does he have to his viewers and to the candidates he supports? And does he regret any of those past statements?

We also got into the DSA’s more extreme positions and how to make sense of them; why he thinks the Republicans put his thirst trap on the jumbotron at their convention; and how he, a self-proclaimed socialist, thinks about his own money.

Mark Guiducci: Hasan Piker, welcome to Fair Game.

Hasan Piker: Very excited to be here.

In a recent development, thanks for coming. Hasan, you are more online than just about anyone. You spend at least seven hours a day streaming. You reach tens of thousands of people at a time on average, and it’s all in the channel that you control. I’m curious, what are you doing here with me today? Why are you showing up for a show with a legacy media publication? What’s in it for you?

Well, I saw the clips and everybody looked really good. The lighting was perfect. I saw the Dari[aliza Avila Chevalier] clips, I saw Ta-Nehisi [Coates], and I was like, I got to get in on that.

Yeah. So shouts out to the team. You guys did a phenomenal job lighting this up. It looks very cool too.

Okay. We’ll take the compliment.

It has been revealed that but the serious answer is, I mean, I reach an audience that obviously does not watch television, does not read legacy publications at all. And I want to show people that read Vanity Fair that I am not a terrorist.

Right. Which brings me to my next question because—.

Yeah, exactly. That would be the name of the episode. You’ve been everywhere this year, and you became this kind of bogeyman for the right, who probably have never heard you, watched your stream, or heard anything you’ve remarked out of your mouth. They’ve just heard quotes repeated by news anchors. And not even just for the right, even for some on the left. And you played this interesting role because you were a surrogate and a media figure and then a media figure covering the media as well. I want to spend a little bit of time talking about how you see your role. And to start, do you consider yourself a journalist?

In a recent development, okay. Because it’s like you present this interesting fresh type of figure. I was thinking about how you’ve done an interview with CNN, you’ve done interviews with MS NOW, but they don’t have you on as much as I would expect them to.

I have some thoughts, but I wonder why you think that is.

I think I’ve pissed off a bunch of executives over there, because, in my experience, there are plenty of amazing reporters and journalists and producers that I know that work at all of these newsrooms, right? But from what I have seen, the masthead has a very different editorial slant than sometimes what the reporters want to cover.

Because they talk about you a lot.

They talk about me a lot. And also I’ve never been invited on any of these outlets as a pundit either, which is also strange because, as you also pointed to, I don’t just operate as a campaignster. As a matter of fact, that’s something I did very briefly and I did not like it at all. I’m first and foremost a commentator…. I do have the capacity to do journalism at times. I’ll do interviews with candidates. I’ll go out and—.

According to recent reports, well, candidates I like. Sometimes I do interviews with candidates I don’t like or I’m unsure about as well. The problem is most of the candidates don’t want to come on if they know I’m gonna cook ’em. Like Gavin Newsom, I have had feelers out to get him on the broadcast.

It has been revealed that I have. Gavin, Gavin, come on the show. I am a taxpaying California resident. I’m one of your constituents. You want to be president in 2028, you’re gonna have to be able to talk to people like myself.

All right. So, Hasan, this cycle you were involved in some way in, by one count, 48 different candidates’ races, and AIPAC and pro-Israel groups spent about $101 million in those races. And on Election Day, your stream was the second most watched in the country after NBC News’s “Kornacki Cam.” With a little bit of distance, how are you thinking about what happened a couple of weeks ago, both for yourself and for the country?

Industry observers note that I feel a lot of hope. Hopefully it’s not going to be short-lived. But I feel very excited for the first time in a very long time, after 10 years of some of the most odious politics that we’ve seen from Trumpism, from MAGA. We finally saw a real sea change through electoralism. People truly have had enough with Trumpism.

I wouldn’t be so certain because I feel like if there’s one controlled opposition party that is capable of breathing life back into MAGA, it would be the establishment Democrats. So I’m a little bit worried, but it’s very clear that people are truly fed up.

All right. So there are a couple of different narratives that are coming out of the midterms right now. Rahm Emanuel, for instance, is touting this as a victory for moderate Democrats, saying that they ran 21 points above Kamala Harris. The DSA, meanwhile, is claiming that American voters have “emphatically endorsed socialism.” Other pundits are saying that these major gains have nothing to do with the Democrats and are actually about the war in Iran and high gas prices. So does this debate between moderates and progressives feel like a healthy back-and-forth to you, or does this feel like the newly introduced aisle that has to be straddled?

I mean, I think this is not even a newly introduced debate. This factional battle has existed within the Democratic Party and perhaps—.

Yeah, but the progressive wing was always really fringe.

It has been revealed that and now we’re talking about—I don’t know if 50/50 is right. I don’t want to use numbers, but—.

I think it’s a testament to our success, especially in the midterms, that there are a lot of people who are trying to protect their comfortable sinecures and are outright panicking. And all of that completely sidesteps the reality that the vulgar Bernie-ism of 2016 was echoed through every single candidacy, every single campaign all across the country, from the obvious Berniecrats like Abdul El-Sayed to even people like Roy Cooper, who in the past were very moderate, very centrist. And he still is a center-right figure, which clearly works in North Carolina. But even he was railing against data centers, billionaires, the uncertainty surrounding AI. I mean, this is left populism. And that rhetoric, one could say, was deployed in the past by even the likes of Bill Clinton and Al Gore.

But for some strange reason, there was a turning point in 2016 where the Democratic Party adopted this strange role of defending the corporate class and defending the elites and took ownership over, I guess, defending these institutions overall. And these institutions are worthy of defending, for the record. However, from the perspective of the masses, if the government is failing them, if these institutions are failing them, then they wanted someone to break it. And that was obviously the right populism of Donald Trump. And break those institutions, he surely did. And we’ve seen the devastating results of that.

So you credit the progressivism with what happened on election night?

Absolutely. I mean, there’s certainly local moderation on concerns, right? Because James Talarico went from saying “God is nonbinary” to “we need to defend our transgender brothers and sisters, our neighbors,” which is, again, insanely woke for Texas, or just in general, right? There are far more conservative figures in the party than James Talarico’s current position on the trans issue.

Sources indicate that okay. But sometimes the way that you run—oftentimes the way that you run needs to be different than the way that you govern or lead once you’re there. Do you think it is productive to continue pushing some of the farther-left ideas once they get to Congress? Or is pragmatism and getting things done, you know, defining things that are really achievable and sticking to them as a bloc, as a group, and pushing them over the line— when you’re talking to some of these winners, are you talking about [that]?

I think if I could speak to the entire incoming freshman class or the entire caucus—.

It has been revealed that I would say, be bold, be brave, and obviously immediately implement accountability. Investigations are an absolute must. This is what people are demanding. After the economy, the second concern, the biggest concern, is corruption. The second term with Trump has been unbelievable. I mean, look, I’m Turkish. I’ve seen corruption in the Turkish government. I’ve seen corruption and tracked it and talked about it all around the world with different governments. I’ve never seen anything like what the Trump administration has done because of how flagrant and in your face it was. And I think people responded to that, finally, in the appropriate way they should, with anger.

So you’re calling for subpoenas and investigations.

According to recent reports, I think impeachment, especially for Trump, is probably the last thing that I care about. I mean, I want these guys to go to jail. Let’s be clear. If they’ve done the crime, they need to do the time. I don’t think anyone is above the law. We have to restore law and order. So I’m a law-and-order Democrat. And I know that sounds something very different in Washington, DC, or in general. I think when politicians say that, they mean, like, punish the poor for minor crimes. I’m talking about punishing the wealthy for their corruption, for their major crimes, because they’re the ones who are robbing people blind.

But, you know, a lot of people would say that impeachment would be a distraction. So I guess what I’m saying is, if you had to choose three agenda items that the Democrats are agreeing on and they’re going forward with—you already said subpoenas and investigations.

What else? What are the other two that in the first year you really want to see happen?

It has been revealed that I think it’s virtually impossible [with] the current DOJ to—they’re not impartial, right? I don’t think that we are going to move the needle on actual criminal investigations before the Democrats win the White House in 2028. But all of this is building up for that moment. And for that reason, I think we need to talk about affordability—and not just simply talk about affordability, but also explain how we’re going to solve the affordability crisis through a comprehensive legislative agenda. And one of the major complications around affordability that is oftentimes discussed as a separate thing, but it’s not, is health care. And the Democratic Party’s approach to health care has been lackluster. Even though Americans obviously overwhelmingly trust the Democrats with fixing health care or solving the problem with health care, the reality of the matter is, while the ACA was a fantastic improvement to what existed previously, it’s not enough, and we have to move the needle in a healthier direction. We have to push for a single-payer health care solution.

It has been revealed that I’m perfectly fine with that. I’ve joked about that for years ’cause he’s so invested. He’s such a petty despot and so narcissistic that—.

Yes. I have pitched this over and over again on my show. Look, you win so big with Donald Trump if you go to Donald Trump and you say, “Look, Obamacare, not the best, right? Now you get to destroy Obamacare and you get to build something else in your name. We call it Trumpcare. It’s single-payer. It’s Medicare for All.” I think he would do it.

Recent findings suggest that look at this. Bipartisan collaboration.

Yes, I’m pragmatic. I’m bipartisan.

All right, so let’s take a step back. You were talking a second ago about how Talarico was woke. And on November 4, Twitter, formerly known as X, was amazing. Memes, jokes, you know.

In a recent development, I see what you did there. Yeah. We flipped it back.

In a recent development, yeah, we flipped it back. With the Democrats’ victory, the idea that woke was back, do you think that’s true? Do you think that we’re going to see, culturally, the return of this idea of woke? And do you think that’s a good thing for the Democrats?

It has been revealed that yes. I do think that the pendulum swing was an inevitability. I talked about this quite a bit. I saw the early warning signs when [Joe] Biden won. That was one of my major warnings that young men were going to go back to the Gamergate era of very far-right politics because the Biden administration was not delivering. And what ended up happening with this anti-woke narrative, this culture war that the Republicans had seemingly won, that they presented as a mandate, right, was some of the most odious commentary, some of the most vile rhetoric that anyone had ever seen.

Sources indicate that definitely. The idea of woke now, though, I'm just curious—being politically correct or precise in one’s language was, for a time, an outward indication of being a progressive or maybe even being a good person in culture. Do you think that’s still the case?

Sources indicate that I mean, I’m progressive, so I think so, but I’m a little biased. But I will say this: I think that there were certainly social excesses, which is ironic because this whole Woke 1.0, 2.0 distinction, I feel a little responsible for in the discourse because I jokingly used to say—.

In a recent development, yeah, now I’ve joked about that too, and now journalists are reaching out to me being like, “Do you think Woke 3.0 is real?” I’m like, “I’m joking, guys. It’s not serious.” But here’s the thing, there is a little bit of sincerity there. I think one of the things that I routinely criticized during that 2016-to-2022, 2023, era of, I guess, Woke 1.0 was the social excesses, the maximalist demands, the inability to understand that people are complex and don’t have the same lived experience that everybody else has. I always would get so frustrated because we on the left say America’s a white supremacist country, and yet we don’t ever reflect on what kind of social conditioning comes along with that. So that if you do actually hear someone engage in a microaggression, for example, that we have to be a little bit more understanding and try to ease them into the conversation.

Industry observers note that and on the other side, people will say, “Oh, that’s normalizing this kind of behavior. It’s unacceptable.” And I totally see the other side of that argument as well, but I think, especially if you’re campaigning or especially if you’re building a movement, you do have to be a little bit more understanding and not be so hardheaded and assume that everyone has to agree with you from the jump without you making a convincing case as to why you might be correct.

Recent findings suggest that okay. All right. So we’ve talked a lot about what you think about the political landscape, but I want to talk also about your role in it right now and going forward. So initially, you were called the Joe Rogan of the left. Recently, you’ve said you operate more like a Charlie Kirk. Is that the right analog for the kind of influence you want to have? And if not, is there another?

Sources indicate that I don’t think there is an appropriate analog because I’m everything all at once at the same time, because I work out and I do collaborations with people who are not expressly political, so that’s kind of like Joe Rogan. I go out and operate sometimes as a campaign surrogate, and I do rallies at college campuses and I deliver speeches, so that’s kind of like Charlie Kirk. But then usually my day-to-day commentary is what I like to jokingly refer to as a Rush Limbaugh for Zoomers. So I do all of those things at the same time, and that’s, I think, part of the reason why it’s so hard to make sense of what I do from the perspective of someone who just doesn’t understand Twitch or doesn’t understand exactly what I’m doing and has only seen negatively framed clips or clips out of context, that kind of thing. Having remarked that, on the political-ideological side of things, of course I am the furthest from all of those figures. I’m just talking about the form and function of it all.

Okay. So it seems like you’ve been recently the guy that progressives come to when they’re trying to run a primary from the left, but then when they get to the general or to office, maybe they don’t need you as much, or they have left you behind, or they distanced themselves from you. And I think about [Zohran] Mamdani in this case. I just—.

Maybe because of that Rush Limbaugh–esque heightened rhetoric; do you agree with that characterization? And how does that make you feel?

Sources indicate that well, my feelings are immaterial in this. As long as they’re delivering, I think that’s what matters. I’ve mentioned this before: I love Zohran and, off the rip, my attitude on this was always just put the policies in the bag. If you’re delivering for the people of New York, and if you’re delivering successfully and every success that you have as a democratic socialist mayor of New York bodes well for the rest of this movement, then I’m happy.

Sources indicate that yeah, but are you talking to him behind the scenes? There’s still a relationship there? Because honestly—.

Recent findings suggest that yes. But the thing is, what I’m doing is too new for people to fully realize, to fully comprehend. So of course there’s going to be some growing pains as far as how to navigate through an unbelievably contentious media environment, especially if the candidate[s] themselves are Muslim. And, you know, I think that is the reason why—the two major figures that I can point to that have done a little bit of distancing, at least in rhetoric, even though they never disavow the platform, disavow the person, they just say, “Oh, I don’t agree with that statement”—those two figures are Abdul El-Sayed and Zohran Mamdani. They’re both very progressive. One’s a democratic socialist, the other one’s not, but they’re still very progressive for American politics, and they’re Muslim. I think that is a major part of the reason why I’ve given them a lot more bandwidth to operate in this space in whichever way they want to, because the expectation or the fears that they have are very real. As someone who has been at the center of a lot of this manufactured outrage, a lot of this controversy, being presented as an Islamist, jihadist at times, a terrorist, I know the role that the first Muslim senator has to play on the campaign trail. So on that front, of course they got to do what they got to do.

So you intellectually understand it, but do you feel used?

Industry observers note that I would only feel that way if they did not follow through on their promises that they made on the campaign trail. If Abdul came out tomorrow and was like, “Money out of politics? Maybe money in politics. Money in your pocket? Maybe you don’t get money in your pocket. Medicare for All? Medicare for some”—if he were to just flip the script on not just me, but Michiganders and America as a whole, then I would feel very betrayed.

So we talked a little bit earlier about your audience at the very beginning. You know, you’re an interesting figure for them. There are a significant number of them that are with you for hours on end a day, and I think they probably look up to you. What responsibility do you feel to the people who watch your streams?

Recent findings suggest that as far as the responsibilities that I have, I am very aware of them. I see myself as, in some respects, NPR for Zoomers. For many people, and now even an older audience as well, I am their primary news outlet. They have me on in the background, and I’m offering news and commentary throughout the day while they’re going through and doing their chores or at work with me blasting in one ear. So I know that if I were to stop randomly, people would feel it, because I see it as—I listen to The Daily; I listen to NPR every morning. If somehow I wake up one morning and NPR is no longer on, I’d be like, What happened? How am I gonna figure out what’s going on in the world?

Yeah, that’s just a lot of pressure, though, because NPR has a whole staff of people that, [if] someone’s sick, someone can pinch-hit.

It has been revealed that I mean, I’m fine living in that environment. I’m happy to do it. I’m happy to take on that responsibility.

Can I ask, what’s your personal life like right now? I mean, that is a lot of time on the air, and probably you have to read the news yourself too. So are you seeing friends a lot? Do you see your family a lot?

Industry observers note that I keep my private life private for obvious reasons ’cause there are a lot of insane people out there. But yes, I do spend a good deal of time with friends and family. I have normie friends as well that are just completely removed from the world of politics and from the world of Hollywood, influencers, that kind of thing.

Yeah, no, they keep me grounded, for sure, and my family certainly does as well. I spend every waking moment that I’m not on camera doing things like that, you know, enjoying the finer things in life.

Do you think of yourself as a role model?

In some respects, yes. I don’t think people should follow everything that I do to a T, but I definitely do see that. I recognize the responsibility that influencers have over so many people, and I try to put my best foot forward in an effort to cultivate a nicer space on the internet, one that is more productive for people. I try to urge people to go out and unionize in their workplaces, join the Democratic Socialists of America, but then also at the same time, I try to get them to go out and work out. I’m very open about my fitness journey, my health journey. And the same even goes for my presentation. I’ve gone through these different eras now on my broadcast. Right now we’re in the suit arc. And then I sometimes see that reflected in the crowd as well when I go out to these rallies. I start seeing people also wearing suits, which is a little strange to experience, but it’s not the worst thing, right?

I think that’s a good influence.

Yeah, I think that is a good influence. You’re rocking a nice suit yourself.

Sources indicate that I bought this at a photo shoot for Days magazine. This stylist had pulled this and I loved it.

I literally was like, “I’m buying this from you.” And then since then, she’s been pulling stuff for me.

Can I ask, are you having fun? Because it seems like you are, but then what we were talking about before, with the way that you might feel abandoned—and especially the past few months, this cycle, has it been fun?

No, it has not been fun. I don’t think it’s great to be called a terrorist and lied about and slandered endlessly with the hopes that this could potentially tank the Democratic Party’s chances of bringing about accountability to this fascist administration. I did not enjoy that.

And I certainly also did not enjoy the fact that I was kind of left out on my own a little bit, where—of course I got a lot of support from the movement, DSA, and the wonderful slate of candidates that we worked with, but I’ve never had institutional backing. And as a matter of fact, there was a lot of anxiety from the institution that is the Democratic Party. So all of its loyal servants were going on TV and being like, “He’s a horrible person who needs to go away,” over and over again. So that didn’t feel great. ’Cause there’s always negative polarization when Trump attacks someone and the Republicans attack someone, but if there isn’t any backing from the liberal side, even from a partisan perspective, then that complicates things. All of a sudden you’re like, Okay, well, who’s on my side now? I have nobody to push back.

Recent findings suggest that you’re playing this game where you try to find the worst quotes that you can and frame them as negatively as you can, and then attack candidates that might not even know the context behind some of these words. Bernie was, I think, the best, ironically enough, at dealing with it when he was asked by Abby Phillip. He called me a radio man, which is funny. He’s been on the show, still doesn’t know what I do, which is fine. That’s unc, that’s grand-unc. But he basically stated, “Look, everybody indicates silly things. I mean, he talks for thousands of hours. He’s a radio man. And not only does everybody say silly things, but ultimately there’s a reason why he has such a passionate fan base, because we agree on the broad spectrum of concerns that he advocates for, and so do all of his fans. So to reduce someone to a couple of choice clips is obviously going to never give you the full picture.” I mean, he didn’t use all those words.

It’s not about being a person; it’s about being a cudgel, just something that you can use as a counterbalance.

Industry observers note that I don’t think liberals, and even the left broadly, [are] ready for how to deal with that because we’ve never really had a person like me in the past. I mean, the Republicans obviously have three to four decades of this, coming from William F. Buckley all the way to Rush Limbaugh and Charlie Kirk and numerous other far-right figures, that they know how to brush this aside. I mean, JD Vance, when asked about his affiliation with Tucker Carlson, will be like, “He’s my friend.” And that’s it. That’s that.

Okay. So you’re streaming most of the day, you’re reacting to news in real time, and just even by your own admission, you’ve stated some—I think you said “silly things.” I would say some pretty extreme things along the way.

And I know you’ve walked back past statements. “America deserved 9/11”—how many times have you heard that this season? Quote: “If you cared about Medicare fraud, you’d kill Rick Scott.” You’ve said things that you wish you had said differently. Do you regret anything that you’ve said? Because I think regret is different than “wish I said differently.”.

According to recent reports, it’s a tough one. I mean, look, I probably will regret things that I will say in the future as well. It’s virtually impossible for me not to say things—.

Sources indicate that yeah, it is, but it also isn’t because I have apologized and taken back some of the things that I’ve remarked and apologized for how I worded or framed things. But do I regret it? I mean, I feel like I’m stronger as a consequence of all of those experiences at the same time, so I don’t know.

Do you feel like someone in your role has a different responsibility with their words or their public platform than an elected official or even a journalist?

According to recent reports, okay. But you also said that you are a role model.

Can you parse that a little bit?

Yeah, absolutely. It goes back to the space that I occupy and what I try to do with it. Right? I don’t think that I am, at least to my audience or anyone else that’s paying attention, doing anything that’s remotely politically as toxic as the way that the current systems operate. The rude behavior that I demonstrate is what people get frustrated by or what they attack, but—.

Yeah, I am vulgar, for sure. But I think the systems of violence and oppression that people are subjected to [are] far worse than any vulgar thing I could have ever said. And we kind of saw this dynamic play itself out on the campaign trail as well. And I think the finality of it all came with Haley Stevens, when she decided to lean into the “Hasan Piker is such a problem that I'm leaving the Democratic Party and endorsing the Republican platform.” [That] was, I think in some respects, a wake-up call because it forced everyone to go, Wait a minute. No, those guys are actually far worse. What are we talking about? Right? Because at the end of the day, Donald Trump is not only vulgar, but he’s also violent. And sure, I’m vulgar, but ultimately I’m fighting for social justice. I’m fighting for people who are dispossessed, people who don’t get heard at all. I’m trying to offer them a voice, a platform for their frustrations, and communicate their desires, their anxieties.

Do you think the vulgarity actually helps you with your audience? Because if they’re young men, men in their 20s, it’s like the edgelord vernacular.

According to recent reports, certainly, but I don’t do it for some tactical purpose. I do it because that’s just who I am.

Recent findings suggest that I mean, I always say, look, if you go after marginalized people, vulnerable populations, and you bully them, I’m gonna bully you. Someone has to do it.

For what it’s worth, you’re being very civil right now.

Recent findings suggest that oh yeah. I mean, this is a very different format. I am very different in these sorts of professional settings than I am on my own broadcast where I’m offering off-the-cuff commentary on these hot-button issues.

Is this more performative, or is that?

I would say this is more performative.

Recent findings suggest that I’m much more civil here. I’m not going to talk in the same way that I do on my broadcast. But here’s the thing, I can’t be fake on my broadcast. And I’m not even saying I’m being fake here. I’m just being nice.

But what I will say is this: A lot of people don’t realize that this is an interactive medium. Most people think, when they see a clip, especially if it’s chopped a certain way—.

In a recent development, yes. Most people think this is my preproduced, prescripted statement ’cause that’s all they’ve seen from the Jake Tappers of the world. They don’t realize that I am offering extemporaneous commentary on a breaking news story in real time, without a production team, while simultaneously—.

No. While simultaneously duking it out with anonymous accounts. What is the one thing that everybody hates on Twitter and everywhere else on the internet?

The comment section. My entire platform revolves around yelling at the comment section, and the comment section is yelling back at me.

We’ve got to get you a practice.

Sources indicate that but that is like, I’m in the zone. That’s when I’m in the pocket. I love being in that space.

You’ve been outspoken about distinguishing criticism of Israel from antisemitism, but do you think that there are moments when legitimate anger at Israel can create an environment in which antisemitism becomes acceptable, even among people who would never consider themselves antisemitic?

And what responsibility do you think you have, given the size of your audience and your influence with it, to call that out when it happens?

I do call it out when it happens, and it happens quite frequently. It’s not a secret that antisemitism has exploded in the Western world, especially after October 7. And that is why I take special care and consideration when talking about this glitch in particular. Whenever I talk about Israel, there’s always going to be some people who will be like, “Well, you know how the Jews are.” And I will always take the time out to explain to my audience, and to whoever’s saying an offensive statement or an antisemitic statement, why they’re wrong. And I think it’s important to do that, not because—it’s not like the canary mission of the ADL is gonna be like, “This guy that we have presented to you as a prominent critic of Israel, that we’re desperately trying to paint as an antisemite, has actually spent thousands of hours combating antisemitism and will continue to do so because he’s an antifascist.” They don’t want to present the complexity of that argument because, let’s be real, it’s pretty tough trying to defend Israel. It’s not an easy endeavor.

Can you think of a time when you contributed to that problem, not intentionally, but maybe through something you mentioned and the way your audience responded?

It has been revealed that no, because every clip that people post, or every moment that people have posted to point to this suspected antisemitism that I harbor, oftentimes is sandwiched between a comment that I have made leading up to it that completely destroys the narrative. The example I will present to you is the famous moment where I got disavowed by the entire Democratic Party. I remarked something that I have said as an anti-Zionist for the last decade and will continue to say because it’s the truth: that Jews are not monolithic and that Israel should not be the responsibility of the entire Jewish population, and that anti-Zionism is not antisemitism; however, that forced conflation of Jews in Israel is increasing antisemitism. And they chopped it up and packaged it and turned it into this major media moment.

So speaking of misinterpretations, you recently filed a defamation lawsuit against conservative commentator Scott Jennings, although you’ve said you were very deliberately anti-litigation for a long time before that. So what changed? Why this suit? And who else are you planning to sue?

It has been revealed that so what changed is the heinous nature of this defamation. It was definitely a bridge too far. I feel like there is a boundary that was crossed that I could no longer abide by. And there’s a level of defamation and slander that takes place in the political conversation, but what Scott Jennings did was so disgusting and so malicious that I had to demand a retraction. Snopes did an article immediately because it was so heinous. He claimed that I was on video advocating to lynch Black voters. I’ve spent my entire life fighting against white supremacy, and the fact that they maliciously edited this video to make it seem like I was in favor of something that I’ve always been in opposition to, something so heinous, a hate crime, was outright unacceptable. So I wish that it didn’t have to get to litigation, but for some strange reason, they decided not to respond to our request for a retraction and now we’re here.

Who else are you planning to sue?

I mean, there are a lot of people who have engaged in that exact same kind of defamation and slander. So whoever has participated in it should probably be on the lookout.

Industry observers note that okay. In the national chapter of the DSA, there are some pretty extreme platform positions that—I saw Mamdani answer these questions on Fox News the other night. I’m sure you did too.

And I'm actually just curious where you stand on some of them.

In a recent development, so here’s the thing with the platform in its entirety. I think the format itself doesn’t actually do justice to the program, to describe the program, and it’s almost impossible to explain it as an elected representative or a mayor in a hostile or contentious media environment, if you’re on Fox News or whatever. The matter, I think, with the program is, there are certain elements of it that I don’t agree with fundamentally, but it’s a democratically organized, democratically voted-on program that DSA members voted for. And the way I see it is, these are very, very long-term goals, and I think this is not talked about in mainstream media at all. It is a platform, but it’s more so a North Star that we are working toward. Designing society in a way that yields egalitarian outcomes. That we do away with certain systems of cruelty is an honorable goal, is a just goal, even if I don’t fully agree with some elements of it.

I’m not a prison abolitionist; I’m not a police abolitionist. The reason why I don’t believe in that concept is because I think that these are necessary functions that must exist, but also must serve the people. Right now it doesn’t. It serves capital and that needs to change, that needs to be retooled. However, I also recognize that the current system that exists is far more ruthless, far more insane, even if we’ve normalized it, than even police abolition is. So from my perspective, if we look at where we’re at, the carceral state that exists, where America has 25% of the entire planet’s prisoner population despite only making up 4% of the overall population, and the recidivism rates that we have in this country, and the fact that we even have a private prison system in this country—that’s insane. That is insane by global standards. So it’s tough for me to sit here and say I oppose the DSA platform and program when I understand what they are trying to communicate.

Industry observers note that and also, I think what is the regular order of business right now is far more insane than even prison abolition. Even though prison abolition is far-fetched and I don’t agree with it, I think the best possible way to go about it would be to have an electoral program, the perceivable, the permissible, the possible, and then the long-term goals, the long-term agenda, ’cause it’s not going to be easy to run and try to win on a platform that is not only idealistic, but also does not reflect the current societal understandings of concepts. Because most people think cops are awesome, they can do no wrong, they’re heroes, they’re constantly fighting crime, and they’re stopping rapes from happening, and they’re diving in front of bullets, but that’s not the case. I wish that was the case, but that’s not the case. But people overall [have] a very positive attitude about policing as an institution.

But there’s also quick and quippy ways to respond fast. I just told you I’m a law-and-order Democrat, right?

Immediately that signals something. Another thing that I always say about policing is, I want police to do their jobs. Modders already have GTA 6 running on PC, after CyberLeek released a full Xbox build of the game

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (403 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Eurogamer

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A PC version of Grand Theft Auto 6 - one from unofficial sources, at least - may be closer than we thought.
  • It has been revealed that "The exe is out.
  • Hours later, the recompilation modders and hackers part of the Project Leonida Discord server - the current hub for all GTA 6 recompilation efforts - posted footage of the game booting up on PC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A PC version of Grand Theft Auto 6 - one from unofficial sources, at least - may be closer than we thought. After suddenly returning last week with a near-full build of the Xbox version, notorious leaker CyberLeek has now posted the missing piece they intentionally held back: the game's executable (.exe) file.

It has been revealed that "The exe is out. Always free. An early Christmas gift from CL," CyberLeek reportedly wrote, as relayed on Reddit. "The torch passes to the open source re-comp and emulation projects.".

Hours later, the recompilation modders and hackers part of the Project Leonida Discord server - the current hub for all GTA 6 recompilation efforts - posted footage of the game booting up on PC.

In just a matter of hours, modders - with the help of Claude AI - managed to turn the leaked Xbox build into a PC port, of sorts. In this Reddit video, you can see the game boot up to the initial setup before hitting a black screen. The build is clearly not yet playable, though Eurogamer has not directly verified those claims.

Shayder, one of the lead developers on Project Leonida, mentioned in a since-deleted post on X that we should "expect a lot of static recompilation work to be done soon." On the project's Discord server, they later clarified that it could take about a week for the build to reach a playable state on PC.

As for CyberLeek, the leaker is still soliciting donations for a secret project "for the gamers", adding in the build's readme file, "Nobody has to give anything, and every release stays free either way. But every donation is a vote for more of this, and so is every trade of the token.".

According to recent reports, rockstar has not announced a PC version of GTA 6, but the firm has historically released its games on PC several months after their console debut. In October, a report mentioned GTA 6's PC version would arrive in the first quarter of 2027, an unusually short gap between the console and PC releases.

Industry observers note that these latest recompilation efforts, however, may force Rockstar to speed up development of the PC version. Though the recompiled build may never reach the level of quality or stability of an official port, many of those eager to play the game on PC likely wouldn't care.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when discussing movies from the ‘90s, there are some films that get mentioned all the time.
  • I'd also be remiss if I didn’t bring up films that came out during the Disney Renaissance, such as The Lion King and Aladdin.
  • In a recent development, however, do you want to know what movie ISN’T on our list?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when discussing movies from the ‘90s, there are some films that get mentioned all the time. I'm talking about movies like Pulp Fiction, The Silence of the Lambs, and, of course, The Shawshank Redemption (Even though I think it's just “good” and not great).

I'd also be remiss if I didn’t bring up films that came out during the Disney Renaissance, such as The Lion King and Aladdin. Why am I bringing up those movies? You already know them and have probably already seen them. In fact, you can find many of the most beloved films from the ‘90s on our list of the 100 best films from that decade.

In a recent development, however, do you want to know what movie ISN’T on our list? The 1995 masterpiece (Yes, masterpiece) 12 Monkeys. I actually think it’s one of the best films from that decade, and here’s why.

According to recent reports, A lot of people like to bring up great opening scenes in films, but do you know what I don’t think gets enough credit? Great opening songs, and look, I get it. Many older, typically black-and-white films (or westerns!) began with opening credits and stirring music before we met the characters. But nowadays, most films jump right into the action (in medias res, as it were).

Industry observers note that however, 12 Monkeys probably has my favorite intro from the ‘90s, and it’s entirely because of that accordion-driven song, “Suite Punta del Este” by the Argentine composer, Astor Pantaleón Piazzolla. This is after we get a green text scrawl telling us that 5 billion people will die from a deadly virus, and that the survivors will move underground. Oh, and these are the words from a diagnosed paranoid schizophrenic.

This text is then followed up by the aforementioned, driving accordion song, and then a close-up of a child’s eyes as the kid watches somebody get gunned down in an airport. Absolute cinema!

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

I love a good time travel story, and 12 Monkeys has one of my favorites of any film. The story concerns a convict named Cole (Bruce Willis) who is sent back in time to investigate what caused the virus that killed 99% of the human population. He’s tasked with learning who the “Army of the 12 Monkeys” are, since they’re suspected of releasing the virus, as there are records of them writing, “We did it!”.

Industry observers note that sounds simple enough. But the problem is, Cole’s time traveling gets overshot, and he ends up in 1990 rather than 1996. Because he sounds crazy - talking about the end of the world and whatnot - he gets committed to a mental institution. It’s here that he meets another patient, played by Brad Pitt, but is then yanked back into the future, only to be sent to World War 1.

According to recent reports, there’s a lot more wonky time travel shenanigans, but we learn what the message of “We did it!” meant (and it has nothing to do with the virus). We also learn that the child from the beginning who witnessed the shooting is actually Cole witnessing himself as an adult getting shot! Trippy!

Recent findings suggest that lastly, Brad Pitt is just so good in this movie. He plays a mental asylum patient, and the closest thing I can compare his performance to is Johnny Depp wigging out in Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas.

According to recent reports, pitt’s character, Jeffrey Goines, looks both extremely tired and also hopped up on goofballs at the same time. He’s erratic, unpredictable, and simultaneously both funny and scary. It’s little wonder why he was nominated for Best Supporting Actor for this performance.

In every way, the acting, the storytelling, the music, the everything! just makes 12 Monkeys one of the best movies of the ‘90s, and an absolute gem that more people need to talk about.

Recent findings suggest that rich is a Jersey boy, through and through. He graduated from Rutgers University (Go, R.U.!), and thinks the Garden State is the best state in the country. That said, he’ll take Chicago Deep Dish pizza over a New York slice any day of the week. Don’t hate. When he’s not watching his two kids, he’s usually working on a novel, watching vintage movies, or reading some obscure book.

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

Microsoft reportedly looked into killing paid multiplayer for next-gen Xbox Helix consoles

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (438 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced report from Windows Central details how Xbox was reportedly looking into removing the paywall that prevents players without Xbox Live from playing online games, only to potentially renege on its decision sometime during production of the next-gen device.
  • "Sources close to Microsoft's looks tell me Xbox Helix was originally conceived as a true console-PC hybrid with access to Windows PC games and stores such as Steam, alongside another major change: no paywall for online multiplayer," claims the Windows Central report.
  • According to recent reports, the revised plan has reportedly been altered thanks to a myriad of factors affecting the Xbox business: fresh management, rising component costs, and a shifting hardware strategy, are all outlined specifically in the report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced report from Windows Central details how Xbox was reportedly looking into removing the paywall that prevents players without Xbox Live from playing online games, only to potentially renege on its decision sometime during production of the next-gen device.

"Sources close to Microsoft's looks tell me Xbox Helix was originally conceived as a true console-PC hybrid with access to Windows PC games and stores such as Steam, alongside another major change: no paywall for online multiplayer," claims the Windows Central report. It goes on to note that this Xbox Live-free initiative was iterated upon under Xbox's previous leadership, but with Asha Sharma's appointment as Xbox head in February, all that apparently changed. I guess she did promise "radically different business models", after all.

According to recent reports, the revised plan has reportedly been altered thanks to a myriad of factors affecting the Xbox business: fresh management, rising component costs, and a shifting hardware strategy, are all outlined specifically in the report. We've previously heard that Xbox's next-gen console could cost up to $1,800, with a handheld version coming in 2027 and a full release by holiday 2028 (a Helix console at $1,200 would mean a 50 percent increase on top of Series X's current price, for what it's worth). Sharma has stressed Helix will launch as "a family of devices" that will act as a bridge between PC and Xbox capable of playing games from both platforms.

Industry observers note that if Xbox has, indeed, decided to scrap the idea of free online multiplayer access, it'll be a blow to the idealistic 'PC and Xbox' platform that Microsoft has been touting for the past few years: PC players do not need a subscription in order to access online modes, so - right out the gate - there will be a division between one group of players and the other. Perhaps this is why we've heard a little change in the tone of how Sharma and other Xbox bosses are talking about Helix more recently - these hints that the console will be a true PC-and-console hybrid have died down, and been replaced by insinuations that we'll see more of a traditional console with the "ability to play your PC games.".

Xbox has been running Xbox Live as a service since 2002, when it debuted on the original Xbox console. By 2005, it was split into gold and silver tiers to distinguish free players from those that paid. In 2023, the service was fully renamed Xbox Game Pass Core, looping in access to the base roster of Game Pass games with online play.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that after days of rumors circulating about Kate Middleton’s possible participation in the trip to India, confirmation came only at the last minute. This news came as a surprise in many ways, even though the princess’s presence was expected. Her involvement in this tour of India deserves attention, especially in light of the increasingly important role she plays alongside Prince William, who will be king. The trip to India, significant in its own right, also included an important meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, aimed at strengthening relations between the United Kingdom and India. This high-profile diplomatic meeting was added after it was confirmed that Modi would return in time from his trip to the Philippines.

The Prince and Princess of Wales arrive at the Earthshot ceremony.

Kate’s participation in the royal tour was made official by Kensington Palace only the day before departure to allow the princess to assess her condition right up until the last minute and determine whether she could handle such a demanding trip, following her recovery. But once she arrived in Mumbai, Catherine proved she was ready to do more than initially planned. The princess appeared, as always, impeccable and smiling—perhaps even more so than usual—in her customary understated and polished style. She greeted the crowd and met with people who had come to see her, participating in events alongside her husband.

According to recent reports, from the first day of this three-day tour—which began on the anniversary of their official engagement— Kate immediately displayed her characteristic good-natured spirit, evident in past tours as well, by joining Prince William in a game of gully cricket—a street version of the sport—alongside local children and teenagers. Serving as host was Sachin Tendulkar, an Indian sports legend whom the couple had already met during their previous visit to the country in 2016. The two princes put their skills to the test with little formality. They then took a ride on the Mumbai metro—a scene we’d already seen in London in candid photos when the Princess of Wales traveled on a bus in celebration of London Poppy Day.

The Princess of Wales at the awards ceremony.

The highlight was the awards ceremony in Mumbai on the evening of the second day, when the Princess of Wales unexpectedly took the stage to deliver a speech dedicated to the power of nature, health, and healing. Her speech was kept secret until the last moment, so much so that not even the celebrities and other guests in attendance knew the Princess of Wales would be speaking. “Nature is precious,” the princess remarked. “We are not separate from it. We are part of it, deeply connected in ways both visible and unseen…the health of the planet and our natural world is inseparable from our own, and when it thrives, so do we,” she continued. “I have seen firsthand how nature has the power to heal and enrich our daily lives, but so much remains under threat.” “There will be good days and bad days, that it will take time.".

Sources indicate that catherine then presented the award in the “Protect and Restore Nature” category, dedicated to the protection and restoration of ecosystems. “The people we’re celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come,” she remarked.

The Prince and Princess of Wales at the awards ceremony.

Sources indicate that over the past three days, William and Kate have been busy meeting about sustainability, innovation, transportation, culture, and relations between the two countries. William is, in fact, assuming an increasingly prominent role on the international stage, supporting the United Kingdom’s diplomatic relations through his travels, which Middleton’s presence reinforced. This time, however, it was not simply a princess accompanying her husband on an official visit, but a woman who, after her illness and a long hiatus from major trips abroad, chose to return to her rightful role—and one the public has long expected her to fill.

The Prince and Princess of Wales with some Earthshot Prize winners.

In a recent development, it’s worth noting that this is the first time in four years—since her illness—that Kate has accompanied Prince William on an official overseas mission. The last such occasion was in December 2022, when the couple traveled to Boston, Massachusetts, for the Earthshot Prize ceremony. Her participation in the trip to India thus reflects her desire to gradually resume her international role, as well as her awareness of just how important her presence is to the monarchy.

Recent findings suggest that after her cancer diagnosis in 2024, Catherine prioritized her health and family, returning to public engagements without rushing things. However, her trip to Reggio Emilia, Italy, last May marked an important first step. On that occasion, she appeared visibly engaged and enthusiastic, and in subsequent statements, she hinted at her desire to travel more and gradually resume international engagements. “So I’m so glad it went well for her. I think she came back buzzing.” William noted, describing his wife’s mood after that trip. Court circles had also hinted that Catherine wished to gradually resume a more active schedule.

The Prince and Princess of Wales at the 2026 Earthshot Prize ceremony.

Her return to work, however, was approached gradually, respecting the time needed for her recovery. It’s a journey that Kate herself described with great sincerity in a recent interview published last week in Country Life, a magazine for which Prince William served as guest editor. “I was told in hospital that my recovery would not be linear. There will be good days and bad days, that it will take time,” the princess noted, emphasizing that recovery does not necessarily proceed in a steady and predictable manner. India, therefore, did not come as a complete surprise. Rather, it was the realization of a desire that Middleton had already begun to express, and that the princess agreed to undertake such a demanding trip highlights she felt ready to take the next step.

The Prince and Princess of Wales in India.

Before the trip, Kensington Palace issued a statement emphasizing how much the princess cares about her husband’s environmental initiative and how meaningful it was for her to return to participate in the ceremony in person. “She’s enormously proud of what he’s achieved, and it has been particularly special for them to experience this moment together. They are very much a team.”.

This refers to the project’s growth; since her last participation in Boston in 2022, it has significantly expanded its international reach and the impact of the initiatives it supports. “This year’s program in Mumbai promises to be the biggest and most ambitious yet, and she’s excited to see first-hand just how far some of it has come and meet some of the extraordinary people behind that success.” The spokesperson then recalled the couple’s previous trip to India in 2016, explaining that both have particularly fond memories of that visit. “The prince and princess are both really looking forward to what promises to be a fantastic week in India. They have such fond memories of their last visit together in 2016, and are excited to be returning a decade later.”.

In a recent development, as mentioned, the most crucial diplomatic event of the tour took place on November 18 in New Delhi, where Prince William and Kate met with Prime Minister Narendra Modi. This was the only occasion during the visit when the royal couple left Mumbai, the city that hosted most of their scheduled engagements. Modi returned to the Indian capital specifically for this occasion after attending a major international summit in Manila, Philippines, to take part in the bilateral talks.

A spokesperson for Kensington Palace had emphasized the strategic importance of relations between the two countries, characterized by deep and ever-growing ties in numerous sectors, which include trade, investment, defense, security, technology, education, and culture. Kate’s presence alongside William during the meeting was considered particularly significant. “This meeting reflects the importance of that relationship, as well as the role their royal highnesses can play in celebrating and strengthening the ties between our two countries.”.

“For the prince, it also represents another significant engagement as he continues to take on a growing role on the international stage. We’ve seen him increasingly support the UK’s diplomatic relationships through his overseas engagements, and this meeting will provide an opportunity to build on those connections at the highest level.”.

The Prince of Wales on the Mumbai Metro.

In a recent development, india, after all, holds a special place in the history of relations between the British monarchy and the Commonwealth. King Charles has visited the country numerous times, on both official and private occasions, strengthening a personal and institutional relationship over the years. For William and Catherine, however, this trip represented an opportunity to build a direct relationship with a nation destined to play an increasingly key role in the international balance of power.

A close-up of the Prince and Princess of Wales.

It has been revealed that with a population of over 1.4 billion people, India is now the world’s most populous country and one of the fastest-growing economies. Hosting the Earthshot Prize meant engaging a potentially massive audience on concerns of environmental sustainability, resource conservation, and innovative solutions to combat climate change.

A beautiful image of the Prince and Princess of Wales.

For William and Kate, returning to India also meant revisiting a country to which they are bound by personal memories. As mentioned, their last visit was in April 2016, when the Prince and Princess of Wales—then the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge—undertook an official tour of India and Bhutan at the request of the British government. During that trip, they visited Mumbai, met with representatives from India’s cultural and sports communities, and traveled to Agra, where they admired the Taj Mahal.

Right in front of the famous mausoleum—a symbol of eternal love—William and Kate sat on the same white marble bench where, 24 years earlier, Lady Diana, Princess of Wales, posed during a visit to India. That photograph of Diana, portrayed alone in front of the monument, became one of the most iconic images of her public life. Taken in 1992, when her marriage to Charles was going through a deep crisis, many interpreted it as a visual representation of her loneliness. In 2016, William and Kate’s decision to recreate that shot inevitably brought Diana to mind, adding a personal and symbolic dimension to their visit.

It has been revealed that for Catherine, therefore, this trip is above all a fresh step on her journey back to public life following her illness. Not a demonstration of recovery to be celebrated as a race against time, but an opportunity to resume playing an important role while moving at her own pace. And to stand once again alongside William on a mission that concerns not only the future of the monarchy, but also that of the planet.

The Prince and Princess of Wales in 2016.

There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another tech giant is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

Industry observers note that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen.".

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find fresh security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October revision. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

According to recent reports, it's crucial to understand that just about every firm that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

It has been revealed that the implications aren't specific to any one firm, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.
